newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli GDP growth seen slowing to 3 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Israeli GDP growth seen slowing to 3 pct in 1997.

text.p: Israel's gross domestic product will grow just 2.5 to 3.0 percent next year, with per capita growth falling to nearly nil, Israel Discount Bank said.

"This rate is significantly less than the potential growth of about five percent annually created by the increase in the civilian labour force and productive capital stock in the years 1996-97," the bank said in a report released on Tuesday.
It said the slowdown, which began this year, was due to the decline in export profitability and an expansionary fiscal policy.
The bank dismissed the view that economic indicators from July-October pointed to resurgent growth.

"An analysis of the indicators...in comparison with their levels from the first half of the year do not support this conclusion," the bank said. "Moreover, the factors that brought about a slowing of economic activity in the first half of the year...continued into the second half."
It said that the government not only had to lower spending next year by about seven billion shekels but also had to ensure that no part of the cut was substituted with new taxes.
On Monday, the cabinet approved a package of spending cuts and revenue measures that would bring the total cut in the 1997 budget to 6.7 billion shekels.

Discount said low growth in money supply, which it estimated reached 0.5 percent in November, combined with falling inflation expectations, should enable the Bank of Israel to lower immediately short-term base rates by 0.5 percentage point from the current 15.2 percent.
A seven billion shekel budget cut should enable the central bank to make further cuts of 1.2 to 1.5 percentage points.

The bank estimated 1997 inflation would reach 10-11 percent, after a slowing in the second half of 1996, as a result of the recent depreciation of the Israeli currency and because of new taxes it expects the government to impose.
Discount said it expected the shekel to lose nine to 10 percent against the basket of foreign currencies to which it is linked over the next year.
